title: Building an offer that justifies a higher rate for Tiling, including floating floors
audience: Tilers and flooring contractors, including solo operators, who quote for wall and floor tiling, bathrooms, splashbacks and floating timber or laminate floors, and want to justify a higher price on value.
learningOutcomes: Write a tiling offer with a clear finish, a time frame, the client's tasks and a guarantee
Identify the friction and risk a homeowner, builder or landlord carries and reduce them
Price a tiling job on value and cost, not only on hours

instruction.heading: A bad offer versus a good offer
instruction.body: 'I will tile your bathroom' is a service. 'I will tile the bathroom floor and shower walls to the layout you approve, with the tiles level and the grout finished, a 5-working-day completion, a waterproofing check before any tile goes down, and photos at sign-off' is an offer. The client is buying a finished, level floor or wall that will not need redoing, and the certainty that the work is checked at each stage.

instruction.heading: The five parts of an offer
instruction.body: State the outcome: the surfaces, the tile or floor type, the layout and the finish. Set a time frame in working days, including curing and drying time before the next trade. List what the client must do, such as clearing the room, moving fixtures and confirming access and power. Add one certainty element, such as a subfloor check before laying and photos at sign-off. Name the risk you carry, such as a fix-first window for defects you caused. Put the scope and exclusions in writing, for example subfloor repairs, skirting removal, plumbing and waterproofing outside your licence, because a written quote becomes binding once accepted (business.gov.au, Prepare quotes, last updated 1 August 2025).

instruction.heading: Reducing friction
instruction.body: Make the booking, layout approval, access and handover simple. A layout sheet, a fixed start day, a clear curing window and an agreed tidy-up each remove a decision or a worry for the client. A client who knows when the floor can be walked on and who does what next will value the offer more. Fewer steps and fewer decisions for the client usually support a higher price, because the client is paying for certainty and reliability.

instruction.heading: Guarantees and workmanship
instruction.body: A guarantee must be something you can deliver and afford. Consumer guarantees under the Australian Consumer Law apply to services and cannot be excluded by contract, and a 'no refunds' line does not override a customer's rights for services (business.gov.au, Warranties and refunds, last updated 27 May 2025). A written workmanship warranty is an optional promise that sits on top of those guarantees. In Victoria, a business is generally given a reasonable chance to fix a minor fault at no charge (Consumer Victoria, Services not done with due care and skill, last updated 13 October 2023). That page does not set a fix-window length, so choose your own window and check its cost before you publish it. Be explicit about what the guarantee excludes, such as movement in the subfloor or leaks from fixtures you did not install, and get advice on those limits from your insurer or an adviser.

instruction.heading: Pricing on value
instruction.body: No source in the research for this lesson gives a price for tiling or floating floors, per square metre or per room, so the price must come from your own costs and hours. Price from the finish and the risk, then check the price against cost and time. A higher price is easier to defend when the client can see the preparation, the layout and the saved time. Government guidance says a quote should recover every cost and add a margin, so check the price against cost before adding any premium (business.gov.au, Prepare quotes). Stepped packages, for example a floor only, a floor with skirting, or a full room with a sealing and cleaning visit, let the client see what each step adds (Jobber Academy, Good, Better, Best Pricing Examples, published May 2021, updated 8 October 2024). That is an older, general service article and not tiling data. Show one clear total and say whether GST is included, as WA Consumer Protection asks for WA quotes (updated 4 September 2026).

procedure: Write the finished result for the room or floor in one sentence a client would repeat.
Set a time frame in working days, including curing time before foot traffic or the next trade, and record how often past jobs met it.
List what the client must do, such as clearing the room, moving fixtures and confirming access, and reduce each step.
Add one certainty element, such as a subfloor check before laying and photos at sign-off.
Decide the fix-first and guarantee terms, and check that you can afford them.
Price from your own cost and hours, then check the rate against cost and time.

workedExamples.situation: A flooring contractor quotes an hourly rate for a floating timber floor and loses jobs to lower quotes. Clients say they cannot tell what the finished floor will look like, whether the subfloor will be checked, or when they can walk on it.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Rewrite the offer and decide how to price it.
workedExamples.reasoning: A fixed-scope offer that names the room, the floor type, the subfloor check, the acclimatisation step, the curing or settling window, and a fix-first period gives the client certainty that an hourly quote does not. No source in the research gives a price for floating floors, so the example carries no figure. The contractor builds the price from his own cost and hours, then checks the scope against the licence rule. The NSW wall and floor tiling page does not mention floating floors, laminate or timber, so whether the job needs a licence is not decided by that page (NSW Fair Trading, wall and floor tiling work, last updated 23 June 2026).

commonErrors.error: Making a guarantee you cannot afford to honour
commonErrors.prevention: Limit the guarantee to what you control, such as a fix-first visit within a stated period, and cost that visit before you publish it.

commonErrors.error: Stating a result you cannot substantiate, such as a flatness or durability claim you have not tested
commonErrors.prevention: Use only results you have measured or can show, and get the client's consent before using their photos.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business guidance only. This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority. Tiling work can need a licence in NSW, where wall and floor tiling valued over $5,000 in labour and materials including GST needs a contractor licence. Whether a floating floor is in scope is not settled by the sources read for this lesson. Check the rules for the state where the work is done before you quote.
Pricing statements are covered by the Australian Consumer Law. The ACCC says misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, Setting prices: what's allowed, last modified 15 July 2026).

qualityStandard: Every tiling offer is written down, with scope, exclusions, client tasks, curing window and the guarantee terms.
Offer and pricing decisions are checked against cost and time, and against the licence rule for the job value and the type of work in the state where it is done.
documentationEvidence: Written tiling offer with scope, exclusions, curing window and fix-first terms
Dated cost and time check for the price
Evidence collected, such as subfloor check photos with the client's consent, and the decision made
summary: A tiling offer promises a level, finished surface, a time frame, certainty and a fair guarantee.
A higher rate follows from clearer value, such as a checked subfloor and a clear curing window, not from longer hours.
Check the state licence rule for the type of work before you publish a price, and do not assume floating floors are covered by a tiling rule.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which part of a tiling offer does the client buy?
options: Your hourly rate and your van
Your tile cutter and the brands you stock
How many years you have been tiling

knowledgeChecks.question: What should a tiling guarantee or fix-first promise be?
options: Unlimited, with no end date and no defined scope
Something you can deliver and afford
Impossible to claim on in any case
Only for new customers and friends

knowledgeChecks.question: A sales page says a floating floor 'never needs a licence anywhere'. What is the right response?
options: Quote it to the client, since the sales page says so
Check the state rule for the type and value of the work before relying on the claim
Use the claim in the offer as a guarantee of compliance
